bib.title: Unsupervised Cross-lingual Representation Learning at Scale
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020), pages 8440-8451

question: What happens to cross-lingual transfer and per-language quality when a masked language model is pretrained at very large scale (more data, 100 languages) and what trade-offs govern it?
hypothesis: Scaling multilingual MLM pretraining data (clean CommonCrawl instead of Wikipedia) and tuning training, sampling and vocabulary gives large cross-lingual gains, especially for low-resource languages, without losing per-language quality.
contributions: XLM-R, a multilingual masked LM trained on 100 languages and more than two terabytes of filtered CommonCrawl, beating mBERT and XLM on XNLI, MLQA and NER
Analysis of the transfer-dilution trade-off (curse of multilinguality), language sampling, vocabulary size and data scale
Evidence that a multilingual model can be competitive with monolingual models on GLUE and XNLI

method.summary: Transformer encoder trained with the multilingual MLM objective on CC-100 (cleaned CommonCrawl in 100 languages, CCNet pipeline), SentencePiece unigram tokenisation on raw text, 250K vocabulary, language sampling with alpha=0.3, no language embeddings, no TLM. Evaluated by fine-tuning on XNLI, CoNLL NER, MLQA and GLUE; ablations use BERT-Base architectures.
method.task: multilingual masked language model pretraining, then fine-tuning for cross-lingual classification, NER, QA

datasets.preprocessing: internal language ID model plus fastText language ID; per-language LMs used to filter documents as in Wenzek et al. 2019; SentencePiece applied to raw text

limits: Authors concede the curse of multilinguality remains a limitation for models of modest size (Fig 4: increased capacity does not rescue XLM-100).
Authors concede RoBERTa still beats XLM-R by 1.0 on GLUE and expect future work to close the gap.
No optimizer, learning rate, warmup, sequence length, precision or fine-tuning hyperparameters are stated; compute given only as GPUs and updates.
Ablations use BERT-Base and Wikipedia, so findings may not transfer to the 550M CC-trained model.
No training token count is stated and no data licence discussion; per-language data skew (English 300 GiB vs Swahili 1.6 GiB) is only handled by alpha=0.3 sampling.
The 2020 comparison set (mBERT, XLM, Unicoder, RoBERTa) has dated; later multilingual models are not covered.

terms.definition: more languages leads to better cross-lingual performance on low-resource languages up until a point, after which the overall performance on monolingual and cross-lingual benchmarks degrades, for a fixed model capacity
Positive transfer and capacity dilution have to be traded off against each other.
